reviews.text: Edit: After playing it a lot more and winning, game isn't anywhere as good as the 2nd and the amount of viable builds you can count on one hand. But I hate the no consumables, HP & Mana pots, Aether Dagger, Stopwatch, etc. They will be missed they helped way more now that I see we don't have them. And most of the temp effects that are given instead on mats are trash and only happen in that single level. Now the crafting system seemed cool at first but I really started to dislike the eternal hunt for letters, in the 2nd game Rift rerolls felt reserved to ♥♥♥♥♥♥ your enemy types so you had a real chance to progress. Now with sharper difficulty spike seeing 1000 hp enemies on Realm 5, I feel obligated to try to force the letters I need for my build. Which usually doesn't work. They just overhauled the guaranteed passives we could get in 2 with the equipments and smacked a massive gambling mechanic in the major power system of the game. It just feels like the only thought to make the game tougher was to loosen the grip we the players had on control in the runs. Being able to craft all the equipments doesn't matter when you've destroy the passives along side it, managing the SP numbers between Spells and Passives were lot better and guaranteed in the player's favor. If you really enjoyed the first two games you should and will probably end up getting this one. But for me I enjoy the 2nd game a lot more right now especially with the Steam Workshop added. If they changed around the crafting system and/or brought back consumables, added a lot more spells (yes I said that, how are you really going to have SIX slime spells and 3 BASE ritual spells) , and some other changes the game would be the best in the series.

Every iteration of this game brings us closer to the Rift Wizard Platonic ideal. I've only played a few short runs so far, but I can already feel that the new systems strike a really nice balance between randomness and control over your build. Every rift is a unique tactical situation that rewards deep game knowledge if you have it, but still allows for analysis and narrowing down options if you're a new player.

Biased because I like RW1 and especially RW2 a lot, but after 30h playtime in the pre-release demo, I think this iteration is a fresh and interesting entry in the series. Apart from the obvious change in artstyle and new music, the mapsize has been reduced, and map generation changed. Skills have been removed (and most of them moved into items), spell can be upgraded twice instead of once (with shrines and item allowing for even more sometimes), and you now gather components to craft items. All of this leads to a vastly different experience to the previous titles. The game asks flexibility more than ever, while also being much harder, not only because the safety net of consumables have been removed. Runs that do make it late often feel much stronger imo, delivering even harder on the power fantasy aspect. A good looking, harder new entry to Rift Wizard with new enemies and design space for creativity. Instant recommendation.

I've put 60 hours into the demo. In 4 days. I need more Useless Wizard's Journal, Entry Two: Everything broke when I fell through that first rift. I lost those pages. The only thing that somehow survived was... my watch? It feels like it's been lifetimes. In fact, I know it has - I can remember me, them, uh, us? before those trials appeared. But, the watch only shows that I've been doing this for 102.7 hours; that can't be possible. I *KNOW* I had at least 90 hours on the clock before whatever it was that happened, happened. The... trials. So, maybe my watch didn't make it, after all. I got what I wished for- a land of infinite choices and magic, with no end in sight. Mountains of corpses block the path, and all of them look like me, in an offputting way. As in, they are me, if I'd made ... different choices, not necessarily WORSE or BETTER, just, different. Some are beggared and their skulls are locked in a rictus scream, and others have been entombed by never-dying (as far as I can tell!) golems who guard my? resting place until they crumble into dust* (NOTE: LOOK INTO NEVERCRUMBLING GOLEMS AS HELPERS??) I remain undaunted. One day, I will master these rifts. Until then, my name was Claire Bennett, and this is attempt number 382724928.

You may be wondering , "how much better can a third version of an obscure franchise be ?" Let me tell you , Rift Wizard 3 may well be the pinnacle of true roguelike gameplay in our current era. Now , don't let the few hours at review time fool you , I've played its demo for 180 hours , on top of the already massive Rift Wizard 2 play time. It is everything we've hoped for , and more. It's significantly harder than previous iterations , keeping the player alert at all times , lest they unceremoniously lose their run. Devs have been keen to iterate on the difficulty curve and added some devious monsters to the mid game and later levels , to keep up the challenge even against the most broken looking interactions that may feed your power trip. Where the Mordred fight was anticlimatic in Rift Wizard 2 , it is now an absolute thrill and will very effectively test your skills. I had to give my all just to win one normal run. While a peculiar change , the new graphics help with clarity , while the shrunken arena keeps things more engaging and edgy. The new music is much better this time around , with custom tracks for both level 20 and 21 bosses , and also secret vaults. Finishing the Archmage Trials is going to be a delightful struggle. Then there's the mods that are bound to show up if I do succeed at that. If you like gratuitous complexity , emergent interactions and spicy challenge , you're going to love Rift Wizard 3.

I really don't like the direction here. I've always been a bit iffy on the series, playing long enough to get a couple of wins and then moving on, but this incarnation doubles down hard on the issues of its predecessors. Information overload has always been difficult to deal with in this series. Understanding spells that work well together takes hours of reading here just like the earlier games. With the new crafting mechanic, you also need to learn the equipment up front, since everything is (potentially) available, rather than being able to make choices on the fly. Given that there are hundreds of spells and equipment, you'll be spending a very long time reading before and between doing anything. Rift Wizard 2 did have skills to learn, but the new system bundles those with the previously findable items, making it far more burdensome. There has also always been an issue of viability in this series – the 200 spells and 300 items aren’t created anywhere near equal. In past installments the difficulty ramped up more slowly, and I could usually find manageable floors early on even if I'd have to settle for worse rewards. So, even if a combo wasn’t good enough to win, I could still have fun trying to get it as deep as possible and make it 8-15 floors with a suboptimal build. In Rift Wizard 3, I start struggling in the first 3-5 floors when I go outside of the most powerful builds. Floor 5 in particular feels like you only have the challenge options from previous games, which are going to result in a quick death if you haven’t managed to get some synergies online. This issue is amplified by two other changes – smaller levels and no consumables. The levels are FAR smaller than the previous installment, and force you into conflict with the enemies quicker. This makes slow strategies and high range strategies substantially weaker, further reducing the pool of viable builds. The removal of consumables eliminates your main option to recover when things don’t go quite as planned, which is a bit frustrating. It also means that builds that are slowly to come online don't have something to help them get through a floor or two until things click, again reducing the pool of viable builds. All that said, the builds that pop off, seem to pop off even harder here than previous games. You generally have a bit more control over how you advance your character, given that you can now upgrade spells twice and choose which items to craft. This means, if you can get past the early game, you can more reliably cash in on the multiplicative scaling some of the combos promise. Unfortunately, I think this comes at the cost of the feeling of discovery and having to adapt to what's available that I enjoy in roguelikes. I should mention that I do appreciate the new art and music direction. While I tactically dislike the smaller levels, the readability has definitely been improved. Further, some crafting components have effects on pickup that are similar to old consumables. You can't stock pile these and they require you to be in a specific position on the map to get, but they do add some strategy to spawning into a new floor that I enjoyed. All in all, I simply didn’t enjoy my time with Rift Wizard 3 at all. I gave it 10 hours to grow on me, and it didn’t. I'm sure others will enjoy the increased demands of the early game and more reliable ability to achieve the biggest combos, but the exploration of new builds is really the only thing that drew me to the series, and that's just not as fun as it was in previous iterations. It’s early access, so I do feel a bit bad about leaving a negative review, but I think the steps away from the design I enjoyed previously were very intentional, so this likely won't grow into a game that better fits my tastes.

The difference of Rift Wizard 3 VS the previous 2 is that now passives and equipment are being merged into one crafting system which you pick up components from the level and fuse them, this is all good since it makes getting the passive you want much easier. But what I don't like is that items are being fused with components as well, when you pick up an item, you automatically use their effects, so you can no longer horde items. In previous Rift Wizard games, if you encounter a difficult level in the early game, you usually can burn a few consumable items and tough through them, but in this game if an enemy is at one health and you run out of spells you just loose. This means you can't intentionally go into a harder encounter for better reward, you either can beat a level or you can't, there is no decision between am I willing to use a few mana potion to clear this harder level or go to a easier level that give me less rewards. And you can't extract value from items that is designed to be used in specific situations, things like turn all lightening unit to allies don't do anything in a level without lightening enemy, Things that damage enemies in line of sight don't do anything if they spawn in a corner. Overall a lot of changes I like, but also a lot of things I don't like, and it is less enjoyable than the previous Rift Wizard games for me.

can we get some player agency on like the first 3 stages??? 99% of my runs end in the first 3 stages if I try to theory craft at all like there isn't even a build yet I just get mobbed by 20 enemies and a bomb spawner with the most ungodly ai favourable map design.

I'm going to say stick with RW2. 3 is reliant upon equipment spam and thus isn't quite as "wizardry" as it should be. I would've refunded, but played too long. Disappointment for fans of the series, notwithstanding the toxic positivity brigade. I'll play till I win a few games and then likely never touch it again.

Whooaaaa, needs more time in the oven. Smaller maps mean everything is in your face right away. Tons of stuns and silences even on level 2 and 3. Who is this for? You can -maybe- RNG your way to a win, or play a 'perfect' build but this just kinda makes it not fun. Previously you could try stuff that might -eventually- not work. I think this one was made for save scummers who like to 'reroll', and so the 'you'll definitely fail if you're not a god now' phase was moved up to floor 2/3. Not.. super great design decision. #Edit# Eh, I came around to it. It's different. It's good that it's different, and not just more of exactly the same. It's just that it's its own thing. #Edit-Edit# Eh, moving this back to a negative review. There's one -CRITICAL- flaw in this game. You NEED components to succeed. Like in previous versions, though, you NEED to pick rifts based on enemies there. If your spells can't deal with those enemy types, you will die, full stop. THis just happened to me, where I was faced with several sets of enemies immune to my main damage type who did 1/2 my hp in dmg @ 5 range... on the 3rd realm. What does this mean? You don't actually get to choose what COMPONENTS you want to pick up! So you are forced to play a grating, yawn-inducing power build of whatever-element-types you happen across, and pick spells based on whatever enemies happen to be available. The items meant to address this e.g. the 'hunter' items 1) cost 2-4 levels worth of components, just for a chance to.. what, have one rift with maybe some of an enemy type you can fight against? 2) force you to lose out on actual stat-boosting equipment, which again, you NEED and again, 3) you can't afford to pick your components. So that's what was annoying me. Dylan turned a fun 'make your wacky zany wizard combo!' game into a 'vaguely irritating case of needing to do homework every 10 minutes and figure out what choices you're -allowed- to make to 'play' the game. Maybe it's fun to train AI on? It's a bit depressing as well, because it shows Dylan didn't really understand why 1 & 2 worked, e.g. didn't really have a solid grasp on exponential growth. What previously seemed meticulous and well tuned is now shown obviously to have been a fluke... oops.

I can absolutely recommend this [i]if[/i] [b]you're alright with a giant shift in this series' design ethos, but it isn't for me.[/b] I leave a positive recommendation because beyond my personal gripes with the game, I still respect the vision and It could even be your favorite entry in the series, if you enjoy this new shift in power. The removal of skills and consumables in favor of component crafting isn't something I personally enjoy over 2. I do enjoy the smaller arenas in theory, but I really just don't enjoy the busywork of component hunting, and looking through each rift more thoroughly than you previously had to due to resource constraints. The consistency of your buffers to get out of tight situations (mana potions, teleporter, chaos bell, etc) are now dependent on a rift's components in tandem with the enemies you're fighting. That's perfectly fine on paper, but It's overall a shift in rift preview vigilance I don't necessarily enjoy at the moment. You were always encouraged to read into everything a rift has to offer, but It feels way more punishing/chess-puzzle-esq to me now. I can't extensively comment on this without overreaching, but it seemed like the bell curve of difficulty is very much favored towards hyper-optimal play in the early game. Resources are quite limited, and it demands utmost flexibility in a way that doesn't click with me, despite spells now having two upgrades again, and equipment potentially being more controllable. My issue is not when your build is online, absolutely not. Two upgrades per spell and more controlled result on your equipment over time, will naturally be fun to play with. I just don't like the patchwork you have to do to get there compared to 2.

Early marketing copy for [i]Rift Wizard 3[/i] gave me a lot of hope that it would solve the prior game's worst problems. I am now convinced that these problems are actually design objectives for the high muckamucks working on this. Despite the smaller maps, each level remains a giant arithmetical nightmare. I have no idea how someone is supposed to conceptualize what happens on a given turn, in this iteration especially because it loves to teleport you around so much that positioning is a joke. I suspect that if you have to know what's happening on a turn then you're already losing because the intended path is to find a build so busted that you don't need to engage with the game at a detailed level. The writing is still outrageously vague. Hire a technical writer. Add tooltips. Do something! I shouldn't look at an upgrade and think, "I have no idea what this will do." At a core level, the promise of a roguelike is that you can exchange time and failure for system mastery. [i]Rift Wizard 3[/i]'s crooked version of that promise is that you'll just steadily learn where balance failed, for good and ill.

I wanna start off by saying that the art is phenomenal and I enjoy the new music and vibe, it feels so much more gritty and grim, and I love it. Thank you khoops for Pumpking :) The game is fun but I think its really different from RW2 and I don't think liking RW2 means you'll like RW3, they feel like two completely different idea's for what Rift Wizard could be. I think while its on sale its worth a buy if anything about it draws you in or you like magic games, at full price I think you should wait till it's had more time in the oven. It's still the same hard as ♥♥♥♥ game, now on a smaller map that I think is a bit TOO small. The reviews talking about some of the oddly placed difficulty spikes are spot on imo. I know, I know, "Git gud", I'm not a crazy level RW player, but I've beaten the previous game and some challenges and I do think that the balancing does feel off. I'm not a fan of the component system replacing items and consumables. Honestly while I do like equipment, I think that some of the components just feel so superior to other components that you almost always want to land on them early. Likewise there feels like no incentive to grab some other components while clearing a level as they just aren't as impactful, making them just boring to strategize around sometimes. Spawners being removed is whatever, Pet's (being removed or less available I'm unsure) I just don't agree with. I think it was one of RW2's better improvements and idea's, which led to some very interesting or fun runs for me. Frankly Tavern's don't spawn enough during my runs for me to enjoy it. I'm unsure if this is intended. RW has also had a (for lack of a better word) understandability and readability issue especially for new players, which honestly is probably the worst in this series with the new crafting system, this could be overwhelming to a new player to the genre or series, and I honestly do think this needs to be addressed. Some Spell Schools do definitely need more spells and/or equipment added and I hope that the EA addresses this (For instance, Ritual Spells could be so much more). When it came to Rift Wizard 2 versus 1, I felt like it was truly a no brainer to spend majority of my time on RW2, RW1 is what initially got me hooked and was great, but RW2 felt like the completed idea. With Rift Wizard 3, if I had to be honest, I think that due to the differences between them, I'll find myself wanting to spend time between both RW2 and RW3, which leaves me wishing for a bit more additions to RW2. RW3 doesn't feel like a direct upgrade sequel, it feels like a spinoff.

The game is completely unfair and unbalanced. I don't care that it's difficult. Difficult games are good when they encourage strategy, experimentation, and learning from your mistakes. That isn't the problem here and it's not at all what I mean by unfair. By unfair, I mean unfair. There are enemies that can blow up half the map, enemies that seem to respawn nonstop in quantities that would make even John Wick flinch, and abilities that feel impossible to counter no matter how carefully you play. When I die, it rarely feels like I made a mistake. It feels like the game decided I was dead from the start. I understand that the starting level 1 SP powers are supposed to be weak, but the enemies past the first couple areas start to feel completely overtuned for what the player has access to. Constant enemy spawns, massive explosion radius, and enemies that feel nearly impossible to kill make the game frustrating instead of challenging. A good difficult game makes me want to try a different build or approach. This game makes me feel like none of that matters. Until the balance gets some serious work, I'll stick with Path of Achra and its eventual sequel.

This is my first Rift Wizard and it is excellent so far. The UI is so clean The graphics are lovely The decision making is intense The amount of spells is insane I am also finding that pull to play another run is very strong. I think the fact that the spell book is basically open to you from the start is really unique. Mix that with the crafting system and the sheer speed of the game and it is a highly addictive experience. Want to add that this game is also an onion, more you play the more layers you find within. The synergies alone between spells is insane Very early into it but deserves a thumbs up

Starting with the goods: Reducing the map space is a good move. Equipment system is fun. Overall slightly better than RW2. And for personal opinion: I get the hatred with meta-progression, but they exist for a reason. Imagine playing STS and being forced to start with modded A25. I also fundamentally disagree with making all spells available at once. You pog at the list for maybe 5 minutes and get overwhelmed and forget most of them. Especially with a UI as hostile as this, there at least needs to be some gentle drip feeding. With the growing list of spells this feels more and more relevant. This game is too arcade-ish to warrant the vibe of Cogmind or DF. For me this doesn't work, but some people like it, so this doesn't go towards the negative review. And the ugly: The fundamental problems of rw1&2 are still there. Lack of a good GUI, QOL, and a intuit read of what an enemy is going to do to you. This series by design overwhelms you, and with the added equipment system it's too much. Even with the advanced search function I still can't find what I want at a glance. Also the search is just broken sometimes? Especially when I'm trying to search by the attribute numbers. There is also no easy way to find conditional equipment (when x do x) because everything is worded differently. I am not spending half an hour going over the equipment list whenever I pick up a material. There is also no way to know what a spell is going to do based on description alone. One of the most broken builds involves putting a stopwatch on a Timestrider and making the leg summons proc its effect. From description alone I'd never guess it'd work. Why is Timestrider the only boots not named Boots-of-? Why does start-of-level proc on summon? What constitutes legwear? I feel like the dev just winged this whole system of categories. Please get a technical writer. While not as bad as say Cube Chaos, often I have to sacrifice a run just to test a niche interaction. The real "game" in rw3 is only in realm 3-12ish. Once you get a build going, you become unstoppable, and all future equipment and spells become irrelevant. The only thing you're doing in the later realms is watching out for when a boss randomly summons a mirror.

I'm late to the series (just got RW3 and RW2 at about the same time, skipping RW1), but find myself loving this game's such basic flow. Equip a staring spell and clear a level of all the baddies as well as the spawners (all the while picking up spell orbs and artifacts). Once you clear the level you pick one of the 3+ portals to your next level to repeat the process all over again (with the additional perk of being able to decide the exact spot you start on). What really makes this game great is your complete freedom in the spells you equip and the artifacts you can choose to create. Do you stock up on multiple cheap spells, save up for a big spell, or maybe get a few cheap spells that you then upgrade with enhancements (every spell in the game has its own unique set of enhancements)? The fact you can choose the portal you jump through with complete info on what artifacts and baddies you'll be fighting on the next level, you can shop around to find a level your current loadout would work the best against. While I only have had a pretty limited exposure to RW2, it would appear the big differences between RW2 and RW3 are the dropping of items and skills for components (usually 1x effects when picking up) and artifacts (the permanent items you create with those gathered components). The components are made of various schools of magic, like one component might be made of Arcane and Sorcery aspects, and when building artifacts. they feel a lot like casting a spell in Magic the Gathering. Say you have an artifact called "Claw of Death" (made up for example) and to build it you might need 2 components of Necromancy, 1 component of Dark Magic, and then 2 more components of anything. The game does a great job of showing you what artifacts you can currently create with your gathered components.

My favorite of the series. Like the previous, it's all about finding the most powerful and flexible combination of spells and items to survive a series of brutal one-screen battles. The third game brings the most polish, with great visuals and music, but also makes adds some twists to the gameplay, removing potions, skills, and treasure chests. Instead, your spells reset each screen, and you craft gear from components you find. I personally prefer this system. Do be aware this game is brutal and there is no easy mode.
This is a sleeper hit series honestly. It's very brutal, complex, has plenty of builds to aim for, and very rewarding. You should really try this out.

Been really enjoying the game so far and is shaping up to be my favorite game in the series! The new search system has been amazing for filtering out things for your synergies and should honestly back-ported to the others. Will say liking RW 1 or 2 may not mean liking the 3rd for everyone. If you're new to the series this is a great one to start with though! This one may be the most challenging though, either that or it's just that it's taking time to get used to the new system and flow of progression. With both equipment parts AND SP being handed out in each level you're handed lots of resources to work with though to compensate things scale A LOT faster in this game than in the previous. I'm sure if you've looked at other reviews or community posts you know about the realm 5 wall and it's certainly a hurdle every build needs to confront, at least in the game's current state. This is still early access so the difficulty curve could see some adjustment soon. Consumables are no more! Not quite sure how to feel about it but I've overall enjoyed the change. On the one hand consumables add a level of depth to how you approach the run as a whole and it's sad to see that go. The on pickup component effects are a decent supplement providing you more options for how to approach and can allow you to hold off spending resources for just one more rift especially early on. It replaces what consumables were most often used for in the previous games, though you can't stack them towards the end stages. As a result I've found more of a need to make more robust builds and have had a lot of satisfaction in making builds that are pushed towards handling a wee bit of everything even if they focus on one core I personally like how the crafting components push and influence your build over the course of the run and find the "on craft" components really fun to experiment with in terms of build crafting. Having the resources for spells and equipment be separated from each other gives a lot more room to explore how different spells can strengthen your build as you progress instead of feeling the need to exclusively stack skills once you have a core going like in the second game. Why run mystic power when you could just make your damage higher with a skill anyways? But now you do feel the pull to get some of those more supportive spells since the resource has been freed up! Also yall if you do find that you really hate components restricting what you can make you do know there's a mod that makes all restricted equipment costs into universal ones instead right??? I mean the game isn't really balanced for it but if you want ABSOLUTE control over every part of your build then chuck it in there. Would say the game is absolutely worth checking out! This game and its predecessors offer one of the best raw build crafting experiences you can get in a game and a lot a lot of the stuff IS VIABLE in one context or another. Scroll through end of run screenshots in the discord and you'll see quite a few ideas for approaching the game floating around there in the builds!

RW3 is a bit like a piano that only lets you play chords; a fun challenge for experienced players, but somewhat inaccessible for newer players who just want to plunk away hitting a few keys. If you want the most pleasant RW3 experience, playing the earlier two games is a prerequisite - and that's not strictly a bad thing. Earlier games in the series are more likely to be on sale; if you find them fun, RW3 will be available for even more fun later. That gives you max value for your money. If you insist on jumping directly into RW3 after skipping the first two games, I'd suggest starting with the "archwizard trials" instead of the base game mode. The narrowed focus of the trials makes the choices less overwhelming and lessens the prerequisite knowledge required to have the most enjoyment.

This game is fantastic. I always wanted to try RW2 but never got around to it, so I decided to jump into this one instead. Rift Wizard 3 fills a very specific niche for me that I'd describe as "Path of Building meets tactical roguelike". That probably isn't appealing to a lot of people, but if that description piques your interest then you should absolutely give this game a shot. Even in early access, I feel like I got my money's worth with the amount of content here. I'm just over 20h in and I can tell I've barely scratched the surface (I have yet to get a win, but I think I'm getting close). Highly recommended.
Its like Jazz, the equipment you don't make is just as important

Gotta love the deep synergies in this game. The wiki is kind of included inside the game but it's still a lot to learn. With all the knowledge I've gained, I'm still a noob. I feel like you either put 30+ or 1 hour into this game. Wish the game was more popular so there were more sources to learn from. As it is you really have to bash your head against it. That is pretty rewarding in itself though.

Let me preface by saying that this is my first ever RW game, I tried the demo and it was intriguing enough to get me to buy it despite the horrible UI (which is part of the reason i cannot recommend this game). Well it took a while but I beat the game and I don't think I would continue playing after that. I was hoping there would be more leeway with what spells you could spec into given the amount of spells this game has, there are 186 to choose from after all. However, you'll quickly come to realize that a massive majority of them really don't matter due to some very common factors throughout the rifts, overwhelming enemy numbers and instant stunlocks for example. The difficulty doesn't really let a lot of experimenting happen. At first, I just chalked it up to being new but as the attempts racked up I still found myself losing around stage 4/5 sometimes earlier until i found some spells that actually work well. Now I lose around stage 10 due to not having the correct components for the equipment that WOULD help. That is another thing. Equipment is a necessity but the system as to how you obtain can go totally against your build. Especially when the enemies surrounding the perfect components completely counter you so you'd lose even if you get them all to make what you wanted. It's a kick in the gut every time and I doubt anyone actually feels ok about rolling into a run ending rift, essentially giving you two options with suboptimal components. The equipment itself, I feel, is also quite restrictive into what you can use effectively due to either use cases being way too niche or requiring more investment into other items that would help but can't obtain due to the aforementioned reasons above. There is also an issue of information overload. The transparency is great and plays well with what I assume is the intended endgame of being so overpowered that the final bosses becomes trivial. On the contrary, accessing the information on spells AND equipment is so asinine and not user friendly that the awe of having hundreds of synergies becomes dreadful and sluggish to learn. The UI is really that bad, I'm fortunate enough to be more mechanically inclined and I still fumble with the menus trying to get what I need. I can only imagine how those who aren't as fortunate would fair against this layout. My victory run was fun only because I got to click once and the level was finished. I could not even explain where the power spikes came from to get to that point except to maybe one item that I obtained very very early. That I can only explain as a miracle. The presentation is nice, the music is great and I dig the art style a ton. Unfortunate that the gameplay falls short behind all of that.
gbdrfes

TLDR- Rift Wizard 3 is an amazing game. It’s hard. It’s smart. It’s chess-y with infinite replay ability. To be clear, this is a niche game. It isn’t for everyone and isn’t the type of game Steam recommends to normies— but if this game is showing up on your feed, or you have enjoyed similar games in the past, it’s an easy recommendation. All of your decisions are meaningful. Inattention will kill you. As will your inevitable partial-understanding of the spellbook. The only major con (if it is a con) is that victory requires a strong understanding of all possible spells, equipment, and enemy behavior. - This means you will die, and keep dying, as you learn what possibilities and synergies are available. — I like that. I think of it as knowledge based progression. But it’s not for everyone. Biggest selling point (for me) is that this runs on the steam deck. ( its predecessors did not). @dev I will buy you lots of cups of coffee if you would update RW1 and 2 to run on the steamdeck.

Love it, nothing like it. Everyone is going to have their own preferences, but I never clicked with Rift Wizard 2. I played a bit of RW1 but put it down after a bit. So RW3 is easily my favorite of the trio to date, to say the least. First, aesthetics. The art style and music have gotten a redesign that work well together while still tying into the previous games. The sprites are easier to read at a glance, and overall feels like a major evolution. Second, the smaller realm size is, in my opinion, perfect. The larger realms could be hard to read and tiresome to navigate. By reducing the size of the realms, occasionally needing to take a dangerous trek mid fight is still a risk, but chasing down the last spawner is more achievable. Finally, the crafting and spell systems. You decide your path a lot more directly compared to previous versions where you are more reacting to what you find. There's still a need to respond intelligently to the resources you find, but you have to find a way to craft your growth at regular intervals. If you don't have some firepower and something to help you survive by realm 5, it's going to be rough. If you can learn some of the basic 4 tag recipes to solve these problems and keep an eye out for the tags in the realms you choose, your chances of success will go up. Overall, a fantastic roguelike that is challenging and repeatable, that rewards creativity and planning without abandoning intensity, and a strong entry in the series.

Rift Wizard just gets better and better with every iteration. The art and music are beautiful, and the mechanics of the game are very well-designed, even in early access. The structure of the game encourages improvisation and experimentation, as level rewards are variable. Spells and equipment can be synergized in myriad ways, making every run potentially unique. I'd say the only small flaw is the barrier of entry: you will die several times just learning how small nuances work, and knowledge of what's available (there's a LOT) to you is critical to success. However, the UI is perfect, and every bit of information is available to you if you know how to access it. Bravo!

this game is easily the best singleplayer game that i've come across in years rift wizard 3 is vast but approachable, the game throws a lot of problems at you, and you will struggle to solve them all for a while, but bit by bit you will find what gives you trouble, you will find how to answer it, you'll learn to speak the game's language and when you do the game will start to click and open up, beating the game will feel natural, you can just "go with the flow", answer problems as they come there are two main resources in this game you'll be managing, spell points, and crafting materials, crafting materials are more /limiting/, you can only craft items you have the right materials for, spell points are more /limited/, you can get any spell you have the points for, but you can only have 10 spells, and you can only upgrade any spell twice. these resources often overlap in what they can do, something killing you? use materials to make some armor, craft items that stun it, teleport away with a spell or just straight up annihilate it with magic! the interplay between these resources is incredibly dynamic, and the answer to any given problem changes every game with every build. do you play it safe and craft an extra defensive item? or try to scrape by and save the resources for the build - up to you. when you pick up crafting materials, they have impulse effects for the floor, some are strong enough to beat some early floors on their own, this does help soften the blow of the difficulty curve - you're able to take the stronger material effects instead of picking up the crafting materials that you want so you can get through the floor with these things in mind, you have so much control over this game that the difficulty being how it is is pretty much required for the game to function, the more you learn, the more you get to take risky rifts to get the materials you wanted, but otherwise, you have 3 options for rifts and a reroll, you get to see everything inside them all beforehand and have the power to puzzle it out, there are no surprises unless you aren't paying attention. i've never had a stronger game recommendation for the /deckbuilding/ and /theory-crafting/ minded, RNG rarely plays a substantial role in /making your build/ - instead, you are more often throttled by the amount of materials and excess spell points you can accrue, the more robust your build is, the easier securing these resources becomes, it's SO satisfying to get to the point where you stockpile these resources for on-the-spot encounter-solving! you can't really run out of stuff to do either, the game is vast and there are many spells to play with and challenges to complete, (most give you cute little outfits now too!!! ahh it's so nice!!) i could easily find myself continuing to casually open this a year on from now. I didn't play the other rift wizards and jumped into the deep end here without much issue learning the game, but i love /noita/ and /MTG deckbuilding/ which i would personally consider similar experiences in many ways. i would recommend getting into this game with a friend and taking turns, or having an audience of some sort to backseat you, because of the free-form nature, differing approaches will always pop up, and sometimes you'll end up with a better solution and be better off for it! (you can even chat in the discord, they don't bite!) i would also suggest picking a spell you like and sticking to it for a while, or going for school-of-magic "-mancer" challenge runs pretty early to limit the possibilities, the decision paralysis and information overload problems do happen early on but i don't think it's to the game's detriment. a substantial amount of spells are powerful enough to get you through the majority of the game on their own anyways! there are some balance issues that i forgive for now since the game is new - some spells and equipment are so universally good at solving their problem that you end up taking them every run (say, staving off debuffs or consistent early floor clearing) unless you personally decide against using them, the game has been getting regularly updated though, and the developers seem very involved, i believe this will be wrung out in time and more diverse answers will be brought to the small pool of stagnant solutions a tutorial of sorts might also be nice but i don't feel it's necessary, understanding the game at first is one of the biggest sources of friction, you are forced to gloss over a lot of text that you can't really surmise much from early... the game doesn't ever /get in the way/ of you learning, there is a help menu, a bestiary exists, you can see exactly what damages you for how much, there are turn summaries, /it's just not always easy to find the relevant information early on/. the game isn't for everyone but i feel like most should be able to get something out of it, if you find yourself curious, you really should just pick up the game and take the plunge, it's well worth it.
